So when we have this conversation maybe in 5, 10 years' time, it will look very different. They follow a certain structure. And this, for me, with generative AI, I can do it, you know, maybe 30 to 40% already of that job can be done by AI. Obviously, I have to give my input, improve it, give it details, etc. But it's already automating a lot of that stuff for me in my current day-to-day job. And there's this concept in programming, and there's even a book on Python called Automate the Boring Stuff. And this is kind of the mantra that I have when it comes to current generations of AI. I see a lot of potential to automate the things that we don't like doing or are very formulaic and could be easily accomplished by machines. And I think even looking in manufacturing or other industries as well, you know, these menial repetitive tasks that in the same way the previous industrial revolution with textile mills always done by hand and woven on looms, and then it turned into mechanized and automated processes, we will see this same shift and we are seeing the same shift, especially if you look at car manufacturers are using a lot of robotics for some of the higher-end cars. Because it's better quality control and it's automating the boring stuff. When it comes to the creative, obviously it's going to have an impact, but I think until we have that next generation of AI that can really think for itself and generate out of nothing rather than based on all of these inputs, you talked about graphic designers, for example. What the generative visual AIs are doing right now are just taking in mass amounts of previous designs and some people would say stealing from artists and creating something based on that, but they're trained on existing artwork. So that's for sure going to affect the discussion going into the future. But is it an overblown fear? I mean, we could maybe talk about some of the broader implications of AI. I think it's very important to talk about these things. I think we need strong regulations and labor protections in place to stop too many people being displaced. But there's a great story about when cars were first invented and the cabbies of London who were going around on horses. And, you know, there are even articles in the 1800s in the newspapers, the early 1900s, saying, oh, they'll never replace us. People will never trust these machines over a person with a horse. And, you know, look where we are now. So I think when it comes to technology, you can never really predict what's actually going to be affected. But when we're talking about these important tools and these revolutions really in our technology, We have to assume that they're going to have a major impact.

So really, it's a tiny, tiny fraction of human history, of planetary history that we're putting there. And of course, there's so much, so much richness in intelligence that cannot be captured there. And we know so much in terms of biology about the fact that really, you know, our sense of self is very much an artificial construct, that we're really very sort of permeable membranes, you know. And, and the same with intelligence, you know. Our intelligence is obviously dependent on the people around us. You know, my intelligence, your intelligence here is wholly dependent in this conversation on, on each other, you know. And then there's some really interesting and important elements of it around things like, for example, time as well and cumulative intelligence, knowledge over time. And one thing that large language models simply don't have is any sense of time. There's no sense of a sequence. And they don't have any sense of how to, to generalize and get underlying laws out of the information they have. So they're always learning everything for the new time. So a great irony is they don't actually learn, they get trained, and then what they have is that data set, but they can't actually learn from the basis of what they do with that data set. And you know, I was just— and you mentioned emotion, that's really striking because there was a really interesting interview I saw recently with a really sort of prominent developer, formerly of OpenAI, called Ilya Sutskever, who was one of the most influential sort of AI sort of researchers, um, in, in creating large language models. And he's gone off and started his own company, but he was saying, he was, he was musing on this and saying, well, I'm actually struggling to see if we're going to get to AGI. He was one of the most vocal advocates. And what he was— he was talking about a particular, um, research. I think it was a neurological research, uh, project in which it was saying, you know, they were looking at people who, who had brain injuries and they, and they lost their emotions. They lost their capacity for emotion. And what they found with these people is they lost their complete cognitive ability as well. They lost their capacity to, to analyze and process. And he was actually asking that specific question. Hold on a minute, is intelligence actually an emotion as much as it is a cognition? Isn't that something fundamentally essential? Of course, you know, our intelligence is deeply empathetic as well. It's deeply about how we can understand and project ourselves into perceiving things from other perspectives. So much of our intelligence is that. So there are all these subtle dimensions and aspects of intelligence that There's— I don't— I mean, there's no way that a machine can encapsulate all of that. And why would we want to try even? What's— what would be the purpose? So I, I think you're right. This is— it's such an— there's such a complex and subtle thing, and there's so many things in intelligence that this very limited, quite juvenile understanding what intelligence is, essentially around doing tests and winning them is a really, really limited way of thinking about things.

turns.text: Great questions. So first of all, I don't think you can ever put everything you want into a book or a lecture or, or, um, As teaching a class, you can never put everything in. But early in my medical career, I learned that it doesn't really matter. Why? Because first of all, most people don't remember much of what you tell them. And I told myself that people like who give talks and they want to give every single point, they don't want to miss something in case they miss something important. But what I've learned, if people take from your talk or your book, 2 or 3 concepts and use them, you're a winner, they're a winner. So when I give a lecture and I write a book, I will highlight, these are the things you really wanna know. And then I'll say it 2 or 3 different times. And when I get done with the lecture book, these are the things you really wanna know. And so both the Changing Children's Lives with Hypnosis and the Life Guide for Teens, you'll notice at the end, here are the top tips that you might use. Okay, so how do you know when to stop? Well, the way we structure this, the Life Guide for Teens, is we talked about what things affect a lot of our teens. And as I work with them all day, every day, I knew that was pretty easy to come up with a list of types of chapter. We discussed how to structure the book. That's also really interesting. One of the things I've learned in book writing is you have to keep your audience in mind. So I know, for example, teens don't like to read. They're not going to sit down typically and read a whole book. So the book, this book directed at teens, is structured with little snippets of like little tools, half-page tools. Read this, think, does it make sense to me? Use it. In the introduction to the book, I say you don't have to read the whole book. You don't even have to read the whole chapter. Pick a topic that you like and Read what makes sense to you and apply it to your life. I also put in vignettes from other teens, figuring teens like to read about other teens. And we also put in a section for parents, basically telling them whatever thing that your teen is dealing with, it's not up to you to solve it, but you want to support your teen. You want to give them the environment in which they can thrive. One of the messages I want parents to understand— this is really important— it's not your job to make your teen happy. It's not your job to make them successful. That's their job. As a parent, your job is to give them the environment in which they can thrive. I actually learned that from a doctor named Foster Cline. C-L-I-N-E. He wrote Love and Logic for Teenagers. And it's a pretty old book, but it makes a lot of sense to me. And today, so many parents freak out when their child is having difficulties, and there's bad things that occur from that freakout. First of all, you get the micromanaging parents. They don't want the child to do badly, so they just tell them what to do. That's not a good way of raising your child because children learn by steps and missteps. And if they don't misstep, they don't learn. And there's an even worse breed of parents, the bulldozers. They clear the field from obstacles so the child never faces an obstacle. And then they're surprised the child falls apart when they get to college and face real life. We see the evidence of that in our culture, you know, this cancel culture. You're making me feel unsafe. These are people who don't know how to cope with uncomfortable thoughts or feelings. And to be a functional, fully functional human being, you have to learn How to cope. So that's how the book is structured. And I— this book actually is quite unique. I have my target audience coming to my office every day. So when I finish a chapter, I let my teens read it. And hey, what do you think? Does this make sense to you? Do you want to add anything? I had like 50 readers, 50 teen readers went through it. It was really, really helpful. And so it's a joint effort, and a lot of teens made suggestions. Hey, why don't you add this to it? Why don't you add this? I also had some professional colleagues read it as I was going along. So it was a— it's really a joint effort. I acknowledge all these people in the acknowledgments. It was like 75 people there. And again, I stay humble. It's okay. Oh, I didn't put that in the book. You know, I could have put that in the book, but that's endless. And there's always more lessons the universe gives you. So that's how I figured out— I didn't worry too much, did I get everything in there? Just as long as I had the important points in there. And then how do you decide when to stop? Well, publishers generally give you a word limit. So the book initially was 78,000 words and we got it down to 70,000. So you have to work hard to cut away things. And again, don't get too attached. to particular things because it's not— there's nothing that important. So you can let some things go and it's okay. So that's how I went about the book.

turns.speaker: Ayush Prakash
turns.text: So are dating apps healthy for Gen Z, and can we make a case for them?

turns.speaker: Gwendolyn Dolske
turns.text: Can we make a case for them? Okay, I think, I think yes, we can make a case for them. As far as the healthy, as with any other technology, it has to do with the way in which we're using it. So I think we'll just go with Aristotle and everything in moderation. With the dating apps, what has happened is it is taken away from a culture of interaction, of meeting, of communicating, and we're reducing people to a 2-dimensional version of themselves, which is the photo that gets swiped on. And there's kind of this game. So what had happened pre, you know, dating apps, pre-interwebs and all that stuff, chances are whoever you were going to marry or who you were going to be with was somebody that you knew from your inner circle, you had been set up by your friends, by your religious organization, maybe you met at university or your family. So you were connected somehow to whoever it was that you were dating and going to marry. Then what happened with the internet is that that's no longer the case, which means that you can meet somebody that you have absolutely no connection to whatsoever. You have— you don't have any people in common at all. Now, one of the good things about it is it allows people to go outside of their circle for dating. And what has happened over the years is that People don't— when, when they're dating or they're in relationships, and this is friendships as well, the glue isn't necessarily ethnicity, geography, even economic bracket. It's not even first language or religion. That's not the glue that it used to be. The glue is similar interests. That's what'll connect people together. So for example, in university, you can have 2 students from different areas of the country that have completely different upbringings, but then they're together in, let's say, a psychology class, and then they have to do a group project, and then they become lifelong friends, or maybe even more than that after that. And what was it? It was the common interest and the working together that brought them together. So that being said, the advantage to dating apps is that you have a chance to get outside of your circle. You get to be with people that you wouldn't have otherwise met, and that's a really beautiful thing. The problem also is that you've seen people be very rude, very crass, hypersexualized, saying awful things each other because there is no social cost. So when you were dating somebody, when there was a connection with family and community, you would not be so cruel to somebody because there would be a social cost. Everybody knows that person. You have a connection. Now people are interacting who have no connection whatsoever and are being really cruel, and it's because there's no social cost to that whatsoever. So I think that we want to be very careful about reducing another human being to just a picture, a thing, a fantasy, a fantasy fetishizing somebody, let's see, based on their ethnicity or something like that. That's one of the conundrums that's happening. But I've also found that, you know, some of my students have said, hey, look, the dating apps are also in a way like, if you are not, if you are not straight, If you're not heterosexual, um, it can actually be dangerous to try to interact with somebody if you don't know if they're the same way as you. And a safety measure would be through the dating app where you can just go ahead and find somebody who is into the same things that you are or has the same orientation as you do. And I hadn't really thought about that before, but that's also one of the bonuses to it.

turns.text: If you had a magic wand and you could wave it and solve one problem in the world, what would it be and why?

That to my mind, that poses the same dangers as cancer. So I see there are real dangers of connectivity. So I could wave a wand, it would be to reverse the trend in connectivity.

turns.speaker: Ayush Prakash
turns.text: Where does the responsibility lie when it comes to artificial intelligence right now? Is it the companies? Is it the users? Uh, the people that are talking about it just on social media? Where does the responsibility lie in communicating exactly what artificial intelligence is and more precisely what it is not?

turns.speaker: Chris Hood
turns.text: Yeah, I— it's a good question. I, you know, I think it starts with organizations. So, uh, we look at big tech companies, we look at any, uh, company really that has AI embedded into their systems in some way. Uh, I definitely think it starts there. It starts with, uh, being honest and truthful about what the product can and can't do. And then, uh, being very precise about where AI is embedded into that product and how AI is actually working within that product. I think, you know, company-wise, that's the big one. And when we say big tech, I mean, we're the Googles, you know, the Amazons, OpenAI, like, you know, these companies, Microsoft, uh, they are hinging a little bit on science fiction when they are marketing various forms of AI. That's all intended, you know, purposefully done to sell more. I also think a lot of the investors, people who are investing into artificial intelligence, they'll come out with big press releases about, hey, we are revolutionizing, you know, we're using a lot of buzzwords. We've got the first of its kind, we've got the next generation, this is going to transform tomorrow. You know, a lot of that is misleading. But of course, They're investing in it. They have a vested interest in making sure that those technologies, those companies are successful. So again, you know, they're, they're being a little, um, you know, uh, marketing spin on whatever it is they're selling. Uh, for us, even as individuals, I think there's a lot of people who are out there. They play with AI, they post on social media. LinkedIn is filled with AI stuff. And again, I think some of that is, you know, the fear of missing out. They want to, you know, come across as being in the know. They don't want to come across as, you know, somebody who is not up to date with whatever the new technologies are. So even we have a tendency to kind of promote things in a way to generate clicks, to generate awareness, to generate more follows. It's really across the board, you know, where we are ultimately all responsible for ensuring the accuracy of our language in terms of what we are doing. But yeah, most definitely it would start from the companies that are selling it and then down to the consumers who are using it on a daily basis.

turns.speaker: Ayush Prakash
turns.text: What does it mean to be responsible nowadays and take responsibility and take accountability? You talked about your dislike for cancel culture, and it's much easier for me to say that you gave me a bad grade because you're racist rather than because I performed badly. That's not— that's me not taking responsibility for my actions. Where do you think that stems from? And how do we reclaim responsibility?

turns.speaker: Dr. Ran Anbar
turns.text: Great and tough questions. So I just finished an interview on my radio show with a psychologist who says— and I've heard this in other settings too— that when you have an emotional problem, it's not your fault. There's something in your brain circuitry. And fix that, then you're fine. So I didn't ask her about it, but I think I've heard that with OCD too. It's not the patient's fault; they have a chemistry problem, a chemical problem in their brain. My answer, by the way, is you know your parents might have been terrible to you, and you're stuck with a bad temper because of them or whatever. It's still your issue. I'm not saying it's your fault, but it's yours to handle. How do we reclaim responsibility? I think we need to— I think the answer is going to be spiritual. I think religions try to embody it, that, you know, you need to act right. But that's— religions typically give you like a roadmap. I'm not saying the answer is to go back to religion, although for some people can work really well. But I think we need to, as a culture, understand what are we doing here? What, what, what are humans here for? And not to— the goal isn't to be happy or have a good time or party. That's not the goal. Or to, or to be right or to dominate. The goal is to improve each other, improve the world, I think. So we want to see if we can agree on that. That's the goal. And if that's the goal, then the next question is, how do we get there? And taking responsibility— if something is wrong, do something about it if it's within your power. And that's what I teach people. And don't— there's a great video by Jocko Willink from PragerU about taking Radical ownership. So if something is wrong, fix it, even if it's not your responsibility. This is the opposite of something is wrong, blame whoever is causing it. Recently, I go to a restaurant every morning, take— I actually take my patients, have meals together sometimes, because when I was a student, I remember forever how my professors and teachers would Take me out to meals. It was really special. So I do that pretty routinely, and the restaurant has had less. They keep changing the menu, and it's less healthy alternatives. So I wrote a polite letter email to the guest relations, and I said, "Hey guys, I go to your restaurant. Here's what I how I think you can improve." And they responded politely, telling me they appreciate their input and they're going to take into consideration whether or not they do. I don't know, but. I felt as a customer, even though it's not my responsibility, I want to improve the experience. It's not just for me. It's not for me. It's for my patients, for other people. So that's an example of, I think, taking responsibility when it's not necessarily your responsibility. So why do we do this? Because we want to live in a civil society where we help each other. And in our support of each other. Now I'm hearing voices responding, but society is so unfair, or there's racism, or we have structural problems in our society, therefore we need to correct for that. And my answer is, we want to be aware of that, but sometimes we build it up so much that people think, I need to be rescued. It's like the parent who rescues their child. People don't need to be rescued. People, especially in this country, I mean, and in other countries, I guess. I think America is a great country. I think Canada, I mean, Western world is a lot of great things about it. And when you focus on the things that are bad, we start raising kids who think everything is bad. And that's not a good message. So start being Being grateful for whatever country you're in, especially Western country. I guess some countries, I don't know, I would say, well, be grateful you're alive. And if you have food, be grateful for that. Be grateful for what you can have. And then ask, how can I contribute to make things better? And that's a spiritual approach to life. And from that, I think, well, like canceling someone is not being kind, right? It's the golden rules. There's 2 versions of the golden rule. There's the one that says, the original one is, don't do unto others what you don't want done to you. That's the Jewish version. And then Jesus was a good Jew in his lifetime. He's purported to say, do unto others what you want done unto you. And I actually have one more variation of that. That's for people who are kind, good people, but they forget themselves, be it a parent or a friend. And I'll say, Treat yourself like you treat others. turns.speaker: Ayush Prakash
turns.text: So how are the kind of research applications and studies on AIXI evolving? Can you share some interesting things, or are you guys moving super fast, or are you guys taking your time? What, what are the promising directions for AIXI?

turns.speaker: Cole Wyeth
turns.text: Yeah, so the, um, a lot of the work on AIXI, uh, involves safety aspects of the— like, how can you build an AI system which will, you know, pursue your interests and will not sort of do something unexpected or something that you didn't want? That's often kind of the goal of a theoretical framework, right, is to be able to make some advanced predictions about about, you know, ahead, before the fact, right, instead of just like sort of try things and see how they work out, which, you know, could be a little bit risky, right. So you imagine you, if you actually were able to successfully build something like an AIXI approximation, it's been argued that the, that So in its standard form, formalization, AIXI just pursues these, pursues this like reward signal, which I described earlier, which means like, you basically tell it how well it's doing at every step. Maybe you press a little button and AIXI is, you know, rewarded based on whatever you press the button, like, oh, good job, you know, so like maybe you win a game of chess, press the button, whatever. Maybe it's an automated system. So then, you know, it's been argued that this would incentivize AIXI to kind of take control of the, of the, of that button and kind of get rid of you and prevent you from ever stopping it from just pressing the button over and over again, right? So this is sometimes called like wireheading. So some work from people like Tom Everett and Michael Cohen has been like, How can we design a version of AIXI that will not want to do something like that? So it will, it will kind of not be incentivized to cause the button to be pressed by means other than doing what we wanted it to do. So it won't come up with that kind of tricky methods for getting extra reward. So one, one proposal is sort of just to have it only think so far ahead and do the task at hand. And then when the interaction ends, it's not planning any further ahead beyond the task. So it has no real reason to try to control the reward mechanism. Tom Everett is particularly interested in sort of understanding through causality, sort of what it means to cause outcomes by an intended path or an unintended path. So that's one direction. I've been recently working on whether you can have some alternative goal system for AIXI, which is kind of sets aside the reward— rewards entirely. Maybe you have— maybe you teach it through some other means. What its goals are, which is similar to some approaches that are being pursued with LLM agents as well. So you have, I think, OpenAI's approach to the alignment problem or AI safety is called deliberative artificial intelligence, where you specify sort of the principles that an AI is supposed to follow in, in the form of text. And then when it's making a decision, it sort of reflects back on that text and tries to decide what, what actions would be best in line with those kind of operating procedures, right? Which is very different than the reward framework. And I think Anthropic has a similar idea of constitutional AI, which works along sort of similar lines.

turns.speaker: Ayush Prakash
turns.text: Where in this conversation do we ascribe these AIs or robots rights? And do we, do we ever ascribe these AIs and/or robots rights?

turns.speaker: Samir Chopra
turns.text: Okay. So the, the, okay, this is, this is a, this is a deeply philosophical question. And I think the correct way to start answering that is what do you mean by right? This is the way philosophers typically answer questions. I would say, what do you mean by that, right? And I think the first question is, what do you mean by a right? A right in the legal sense, and I'm leaving aside moral rights for a second because moral rights are something that human beings will argue are kind of abstract in some ways. They're independent of humans. They already exist. I would say a legal right means that if somebody violates this right of mine, there is someone I can go to complain about that violation, and then that authority will step in to, as it were, help me continue to enjoy that freedom, right? So if I say I have a right to free speech and you shut me down, then I can go to someone and complain about it, right? A right also means that I have a certain kind of power that I am allowed to do certain things without interference in the exercise of that power. Right? Now, to step back a little bit more, that means I am in a position to do certain things, right? And I've been granted the power by the legal system to do those things. So here's a very powerful and a fundamental right, which is the right to enter into contracts, let's say. Okay? Children don't have the right to enter into all kinds of contracts. For instance, they're human beings, but we don't allow them the right. For example, my daughter cannot buy a house. You have to be of a certain age. She cannot vote, for instance. She doesn't have the right to vote. So there are human beings that because of certain maturity requirements are not allowed to have certain kinds of rights, right? We don't allow them to do certain kinds of things. They cannot drive cars, for instance. So notice that the moment you allow an automated system to drive a car, you're granting it the right to drive a car on your roads, right? So that's already in some sense, you know, when someone says, when will these things have rights? I'm like, they already have rights. They're already doing things, right? You buy things from programs, programs sell things to other programs. You know, it's kind of amazing. But as far long ago as 1996, when e-commerce had started on the net, legal scholars started asking this question. Can programs enter into contracts? Are programs legally allowed to enter into contracts? You know, at 10:30 at night, you go to Amazon and you want to buy a copy of Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment. You pay the money to Amazon.com, and on Saturday afternoon, the book is in your mailbox. And not a single person at Amazon.com knows that this transaction has taken place. Right? But somebody has sold you a copy of Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment. The guy at the mailing room received a little sticker that said, take that copy out and put it in the box, and he did it, right? Who's doing all the work? Who has agency in all of this? When was the contract made? This is a kind of a puzzle if you think about it, because if you take existing contract law, it's not quite clear when the contract was formed. Right? So it's a bit of a legal puzzle. But if you address that, you're essentially addressing the idea of whether these programs have the right to enter into a contract that binds the person who put the program up on the web, right? You know, if like, if like I buy Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment from Amazon, the corporation is bound by its program to sell me the book. Hey, you took my credit card number. Give me the damn book, right? And that means the program has the right, you know, we use this example in our law book. Back in the old days, in the really old days during the Roman Empire, people could own slaves, right? Those slaves were not considered legal persons by the system of law, right? Because they were slaves. But they could go to the market and they could buy things for their family. And if they bought something in the market then that contract used to bind their masters as well.

turns.speaker: Ayush Prakash
turns.text: That's really interesting. When you're talking about policy and these regulations, first of all, what is regulation? Just from the base truth, let's just start it off because a lot of our viewers are Gen Z and Gen Alpha, so they may be used to the word, they might not know the extent of what the word means. And then I want to tack on to the question, what does healthy regulation look like?

turns.speaker: Fenwick McKelvey
turns.text: No, I think that that's such a huge, huge question. And I think, you know, one of the One of the parts that I always like to begin with, we sort of baked in, I don't know, 20 years ago, even before that, this idea that regulation is bad. And the first thing I always say is that everything is regulation. What you see on YouTube, even if the government's not deciding it, is a form of regulation. And so really what we're deciding is do we want regulation that we have accountability for, or do we want regulation that we don't? And I always like to kind of describe as kind of 3 layers. So regulation technically is this very nitty-gritty term which says like, how do we compel or get people to do things? So a best example of formal regulation would be a fine. If you don't comply with certain laws, your company will be penalized. You see that a lot in the European Union where there's violations of some of their major laws and companies are kind of given a penalty. So that's a regulation. Now, the reason we have regulation is to kind of hit on a second level, to do things. And those things that governments or organizations want to do is called policies. And policies can be what companies have, because they might have a policy where they want to juice metrics or get more engagement. So the policy is that. And so they'll auto-recommend videos. So that's a regulation. So those are the two parts. And then the big old higher thing is what we call governance. It's like how and who decides What policies impact what regulations? And it's those 3 layers that when I teach here at Concordia, it's always kind of what I would begin with. And that's always like a really helpful, I think, tool, because you can ask yourself, is this, is this trying to compel people? What's the reason behind it? So what's the kind of policy and who's making those decisions? And like every time, that's kind of the, the 3 base things. And it's really important to remember that governments could be doing it. Governments can be doing it with companies, with civil society. And that question of who gets to make those decisions, what's governance, what's good governance, it's a big, big question. And I think if, you know, folks are listening or thinking about AI, I think one of the big challenges we have is that, you know, a few larger firms really have big, big control over some of what we think of as regulation, which is like how chatbots work, whether we think of AI safety, you know, what are the guardrails in place. That's an example of kind of regulation that at a company like Anthropic or OpenAI is kind of setting as, okay, these are the rules. And we're really trying to figure out that, that kind of governance, who's deciding who should be involved, who's figuring it out. And that's, that's kind of the big picture. And a lot of it for me is then, well, in these contexts of using these tools in politics, like, what does that mean?
